title: Samana, 1709
hookLine: Banda's growing army takes Samana, home of those who executed Guru Tegh Bahadur

cards: A question with no comfortable answer. If someone had killed a person you loved, and years later you had the power to reach them, what would you call what you did next?
In Punjab, people began to gather around Banda Singh: farmers, villagers, Sikhs who had read the Guru's letters. His following grew into an army. And the town it struck early on was Samana.
Tradition says Samana was home to the men who had carried out the execution of Guru Tegh Bahadur.

teach.b: Sikh tellings remember Samana as the place where Banda Singh's campaign began to answer the wrongs done to the Gurus. The town was taken by force.
Accounts of that day are harsh, and they don't agree on every detail. That honesty belongs in the story: a path that remembers its own martyrs carefully should remember a fallen town carefully too.
So what does justice, not revenge, mean? Start with the opening lines of the Guru Granth Sahib.

teach.h: NIRBHAU, NIRVAIR: NO FEAR, NO ENMITY.
teach.b: Those words, the Mul Mantar, describe the One as nirbhau and nirvair: without fear, and without enmity. Japji, a morning prayer, begins with them.
No hatred lives in the One they turn toward, and that sets a hard standard for anyone who picks up a sword in the Guru's name. Here is one way to hear the difference.
Revenge looks backward and spreads; it wants the other side to hurt the way you hurt, and it rarely knows when to stop.
Justice looks at a specific wrong, aims at the ones responsible, and is meant to end. Sikh tellings hold that the sword is lifted only to stop oppression, not to feed a grudge.

Some readers hold Banda Singh's campaign up to that standard and honor it. Others ask hard questions about what happened to ordinary people in the towns that fell. Both are part of how this story is told.
What doesn't change is the line the Mul Mantar draws: whatever you do, you are not meant to do it from hatred.

how: Sikhs remember Samana as an early town taken in Banda Singh Bahadur's campaign, and often discuss it alongside the Gurus' teaching that force may be used only against oppression and never from hatred.

practice: Bring to mind a wrong done to you or to someone you love: not the worst one, one you can hold for two minutes.
Ask quietly what would make it right, then what would only make them hurt, and notice that the two answers differ, and which one your body leans toward.
You don't have to settle anything; if you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out.
